title: Xanthe and the Summer
premise: Tamsin Amberdale has spent twelve years raising her daughter alone behind the counter of the only bookshop in Aldercombe, a village wrapped around the failing Halcyon vineyard. When a freak June snowstorm traps her overnight with Julian Voss—the vineyard's new owner and the man she loved at twenty-two—and his ruthless business rival Marcus Hale, old truths surface: Julian left her pregnant and unknowing, and Marcus has been quietly buying the town's debts, including hers. As harvest approaches, Tamsin must choose between selling the bookshop to secure her daughter's future and trusting Julian with a second chance, while Marcus weaponizes her secret to force the sale. In the end she refuses both men's terms, exposes Marcus's coercion to the town, and builds something new—keeping the shop, accepting Julian's slow courtship rather than a rescue, and letting the first harvest be a beginning instead of an ending.
about_author: Marguerite Oyelaran is a former sommelier turned novelist who writes love stories set in working landscapes, where romance and livelihood are inseparable. She lives between a coastal city and her partner's family orchard, where she claims to research but mostly over-prunes.

chapters.title: The Weight of Ordinary Days
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A morning in Aldercombe: opening the bookshop, school-run chaos with twelve-year-old Wren, small-town rhythms established. We learn she measures life in safe steps since a heartbreak she won't name. Beat: contentment that feels slightly like anesthesia.

chapters.title: Letters from the New Owner
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. News arrives that Halcyon vineyard has been sold to an English investor named Julian Voss. Tamsin goes cold at the name but tells no one why. Her landlord mentions new interest in buying the shop's building. Beat: dread disguised as curiosity.

chapters.title: Marcus Hale Comes to Town
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. The rival arrives—charming, precise, buying up property quietly through intermediaries. He meets Tamsin at the shop and is genuinely disarmed by her. He recognizes Julian's history here and files it away as leverage. Beat: charm with a blade under it.

chapters.title: Twelve Years Ago
chapters.summary: Julian's POV, flashback woven into present. He returns to Aldercombe after a decade abroad, walking streets he fled at twenty-four when his father demanded he take over the family wine empire instead of staying with a bookseller's daughter. Beat: guilt arriving before the man does.

chapters.title: The Reunion Nobody Planned
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Julian walks into the bookshop to introduce himself to the town. They face each other across a display table; Wren appears, unmistakably his daughter's age. Neither says it. Beat: the floor dropping out while both pretend to stand still.

chapters.title: Snow in June
chapters.summary: Multiple POV. An unseasonal storm strands a festival-planning meeting—Tamsin, Julian, and Marcus—at the vineyard house overnight. Power fails, wine comes out, and Marcus watches the two of them orbit each other like dying stars. Beat: forced intimacy, guarded words.

chapters.title: What the Firelight Said
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. By candlelight, Julian almost confesses about Wren; Tamsin cuts him off, saying some accounts are closed. Marcus, sleepless, overhears enough—a child, a date—to start assembling the truth. Beat: the past knocking louder than either will answer.

chapters.title: Wren's Question
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Wren, sharp-eyed, asks why the new vineyard man looks at her 'like a math problem.' Tamsin deflects badly. Meanwhile Marcus makes a generous offer for the shop building—too generous. Beat: mother-love colliding with buried truth.

chapters.title: The Arithmetic of Debts
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus reveals to Tamsin that he holds the note on her building and offers forgiveness in exchange for her support against Julian's plans—or silence about what he suspects. She realizes how trapped she is. Beat: power showing its polite face.

chapters.title: Vines and Verities
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Julian, restoring the vineyard, finds his father's old ledger and learns the estate was already failing when he was pushed to leave—that his sacrifice bought nothing. He rages, then resolves to build something honest here. Beat: grief turning into purpose.

chapters.title: A Second First Date
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Julian asks for nothing except time: they walk the harvest rows, talk like adults, and Tamsin lets herself feel hope for one evening. Coming home, she finds Marcus waiting with the debt papers. Beat: joy interrupted at the door.

chapters.title: The Ultimatum
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Marcus lays it out: sign the sale, publicly back his development plan, or he tells Julian about Wren first—framing her concealment as gold-digging. She signs nothing but says nothing either, protecting Wren above all. Beat: duty tightening its grip.

chapters.title: Daughter of the Shopkeeper
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren does her own investigating—library records, a birth certificate left carelessly out—and confronts her mother: 'Is he my dad?' Tamsin finally tells the truth. Beat: the secret leaving the vault, tenderly, on Wren's terms.

chapters.title: Meeting His Mirror
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. Wren shows up at the vineyard alone, having worked it out, and asks blunt questions. Julian, floored, answers every one honestly. They agree to tell Tamsin together—but Marcus sees them and moves first. Beat: connection blooming under threat.

chapters.title: Poisoned Vintage
chapters.summary: Multiple POV. At the town festival, Marcus announces the development plan and insinuates that Tamsin has been trading influence with Julian—implying scandal. Julian defends her fiercely without knowing the full truth; Tamsin flees. Beat: public humiliation, private fury.

chapters.title: The Fight That Was Owed
chapters.summary: Tamsin and Julian's alternating POV. Finally alone, they have the twelve-years-late fight: his leaving, her silence about Wren, his father's cruelty, her pride. Everything true gets said. It ends not in reconciliation but in exhausted honesty. Beat: catharsis before repair.

chapters.title: Harvest Eve
chapters.summary: Julian's POV. On the eve of first harvest, Marcus presents Julian with an ultimatum too: abandon the town project or he releases documents painting Tamsin as a schemer who hid an heir for leverage. Julian chooses Tamsin and Wren outright, telling Marcus to do his worst. Beat: love choosing itself against power.

chapters.title: The Town Meeting
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Marcus plays his card publicly—but Tamsin stands before the whole town and tells her own story first: Wren, the abandonment, the coercion, the debt. The town, which knew more than anyone admitted, turns on Marcus. Beat: reclaiming the narrative at cost.

chapters.title: What Marcus Wanted
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Defeated, Marcus reveals a sliver of his own wound—he was once the boy whose family lost everything to a town's indifference—and leaves Aldercombe, selling Tamsin's debt at par to Julian with no strings. Beat: villain humanized, not redeemed.

chapters.title: First Harvest
chapters.summary: Multiple POV. The whole town picks grapes at dawn; Wren works beside Julian awkwardly, wonderfully. Tamsin watches her daughter and the man who came back share something she can't orchestrate or control. Beat: abundance after scarcity.

chapters.title: Not a Rescue
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Julian offers everything—house, security, the debts cleared—and Tamsin declines the package, choosing instead a slower thing: dating, partnership, keeping her shop and her name. He laughs, relieved, and agrees. Beat: love redefined as choice, not salvation.

chapters.title: Xanthe and the Summer
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Tamsin's POV. Autumn: the first vintage is bottled—Julian names it Xanthe, the Greek word for golden, after the summer everything changed. In the bookshop, Wren shelves a novel her mother wrote; Julian reads in the window seat. Beat: a life measured no longer in safe steps, but in chosen ones.
